cues.speaker: ED
cues.text: Today I'm going to talk about the eucalyptus tree.

cues.speaker: ED
cues.text: This is a very common tree here in Australia, where it's also sometimes called the gum

cues.speaker: ED
cues.text: tree.

cues.speaker: ED
cues.text: First I'm going to talk about why it's important, then I'm going to describe some

cues.speaker: ED
cues.text: problems it faces at present.

cues.speaker: ED
cues.text: Right, well the eucalyptus tree is an important tree for lots of reasons.

cues.speaker: ED
cues.text: For example, it gives shelter to creatures like birds and bats, and these and other

cues.speaker: ED
cues.text: species also depend on it for food, particularly the nectar from its flowers.

cues.speaker: ED
cues.text: So it supports biodiversity.

cues.speaker: ED
cues.text: It's useful to us humans too, because we can kill germs with a disinfectant made from oil

cues.speaker: ED
cues.text: extracted from eucalyptus leaves.

cues.speaker: ED
cues.text: The eucalyptus grows all over Australia and the trees can live for up to four hundred

cues.speaker: ED
cues.text: years.

cues.speaker: ED
cues.text: So it's alarming that all across the country, numbers of eucalyptus are falling because

cues.speaker: ED
cues.text: the trees are dying off prematurely. So what are the reasons for this?

cues.speaker: ED
cues.text: One possible reason is disease.

cues.speaker: ED
cues.text: As far back as the 1970s the trees started getting a disease called Mundulla Yellows.

cues.speaker: ED
cues.text: The trees' leaves would gradually turn yellow, then the tree would die.

cues.speaker: ED
cues.text: It wasn't until 2004 that they found the cause of the problem was lime, or calcium

cues.speaker: ED
cues.text: hydroxide to give it its proper chemical name, which was being used in the construction

cues.speaker: ED
cues.text: of roads.

cues.speaker: ED
cues.text: The lime was being washed away into the ground and affecting the roots of the eucalyptus

cues.speaker: ED
cues.text: trees nearby.

cues.speaker: ED
cues.text: What is was doing was preventing the trees from sucking up the iron they needed for

cues.speaker: ED
cues.text: healthy growth.

cues.speaker: ED
cues.text: When this was injected back into the affected trees, they immediately recovered.

cues.speaker: ED
cues.text: But this problem only affected a relatively small number of trees.

cues.speaker: ED
cues.text: By 2000, huge numbers of eucalyptus were dying along Australia's East Coast, of a disease

cues.speaker: ED
cues.text: known as Bell-miner Associated Die-back.

cues.speaker: ED
cues.text: The bell-miner is a bird, and the disease seems to be common where there are high

cues.speaker: ED
cues.text: populations of bell-miners. Again it's the leaves of the trees that are affected.

cues.speaker: ED
cues.text: What happens is that insects settle on the leaves and eat their way round them,

cues.speaker: ED
cues.text: destroying them as they go, and at the same time they secrete a solution which has sugar

cues.speaker: ED
cues.text: in it.

cues.speaker: ED
cues.text: The bell-miner birds really like this solution, and in order to get as much as possible,

cues.speaker: ED
cues.text: they keep away other creatures that might try to get it.

cues.speaker: ED
cues.text: So these birds and insects flourish at the expense of other species, and eventually so

cues.speaker: ED
cues.text: much damage is done to the leaves that the tree dies.
